what_it_does: Running AI models for inference (answering questions based on trained weights) requires moving enormous amounts of data between a processor's math units and its memory. A typical GPU spends most of its time waiting to fetch data rather than actually computing, and that data movement consumes more power than the compute itself. CORSAIR is a new chip architecture that brings computation closer to the data by using small, independent computing modules called chiplets that integrate analog or mixed-signal in-memory computing fabric—essentially, tiny specialized circuits built directly into the memory chips themselves. Instead of fetching matrix elements into the GPU to multiply them, the multiplication happens right inside the memory where the data lives. The chiplets connect to each other through standard links, so different parts can be swapped or upgraded without redesigning the whole chip. This approach trades some complexity in the memory fabric for dramatically lower power consumption and latency during the matrix multiplications that dominate AI inference.
